newsitem.title: UGANDA: U.S. "green berets" to land in Uganda as trainers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "green berets" to land in Uganda as trainers.

text.p: More than 100 U.S. troops including "green berets" arrive in Uganda on Monday to train Ugandan soldiers for a continental peacekeeping force, U.S. officials said.
The U.S. Information Service said 120 U.S. troops would land at Entebbe airport on Monday evening in two groups to start training a Ugandan battalion later this month for peacekeeping duties.

The 120 trainers are mostly from the Third Special Forces Group in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and are being sent in response to a so-called African Crisis Response Initiative (ACRI), which Washington has been developing since last year.
Washington has said U.S. trainers would also be sent to Senegal this week.

U.S. officials said the initiative sought to create highly effective and rapidly deployable peacekeeping units to operate jointly during humanitarian crises on the world's poorest continent or when a peacekeeping operation was necessary.
Training is based on a common peacekeeping doctrine and U.S. communications equipment will allow units to work together.
Training is expected soon to start in other African countries, possibly including Tunisia, Ethiopia, Mali and Ghana.
Proposals for an African peacekeeping force were developed by the United States and Organisation of African Unity after the international failure to prevent genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
An estimated 800,000 members of the Tutsi minority and Hutu moderates were slaughtered during a three-month genocide in Rwanda in 1994 until Tutsi rebels, backed by Uganda, seized power.
U.N. troops based at the time in Rwanda, which borders on Uganda, failed to intervene to halt the genocide by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs because it was outside their U.N. mandate.
The U.S. troops will train Ugandans for peacekeeping and take part in annual joint exercises between the U.S. military and the government Ugandan People's Defence Force (UPDF).
Since the Rwandan genocide, the United States has stressed that African problems should be handled by Africans themselves.

U.S. troops took part in international aid to Rwanda in the wake of the genocide but were based in Uganda. The U.S. military also searched by plane for Rwandan refugees scattered by civil war in the former Zaire in 1996, again from a base in Uganda.
The first African peacekeeping military exercises were held in Zimbabwe in April involving troops from Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania and Zimbabwe.
South Africa and Kenya insist any African peacekeeping force should be all African because of fears that in a crisis command and control would fall into foreign hands while Africans did the fighting.
